Mizmor
miz-MOR
noun
Hebrew mizmōr, from zāmar, “to make music, to sing praise with instruments, to pluck the strings”; a song set to music — the very word the English “Psalm” translates.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

📖 Biblical Definition

Mizmor is the Hebrew word that the English “Psalm” renders, standing in the title of some fifty-seven psalms, as “A Psalm of David” (Psa 23, title) or simply “A Psalm” (Psa 98, title). It comes of a root meaning to make music, to praise with instruments, to pluck the sounding strings; and so a mizmor is not bare speech but a song framed and set to music for the worship of God. The Greek translators rendered it psalmos, whence comes our word Psalter, the book of praises. The thing itself teaches a doctrine: that God is to be praised with skill and with melody, the truth carried upon a tune, the heart lifted by the consecrated art of song. “Let us come before his presence with thanksgiving, and make a joyful noise unto him with psalms” (Psa 95:2). This is no relic of an outgrown age; the apostle binds the same threefold cord upon the church, “speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Eph 5:19). The mizmor abides: the people of God are a singing people, and the inspired Psalter is their first and surest songbook, the very mind of the Spirit set to music for the praise of the Most High.

📖 Key Scripture

Psa 23, title — "A Psalm of David."

Psa 98, title — "A Psalm. O sing unto the LORD a new song; for he hath done marvellous things."

Psa 95:2 — "Let us come before his presence with thanksgiving, and make a joyful noise unto him with psalms."

Eph 5:19 — "Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The very word “Psalm”; it recovers sung, skilful, congregational praise and the primacy of the inspired Psalter against worship reduced to mere talk or mere spectacle.

expand to see more

Mizmor faces no postmodern redefinition, but the practice it commands is pulled two ways in the present age — toward a bare and songless religion that reduces worship to talk, and toward a spectacle that prizes performance above the praise of the gathered people. The word answers both: a mizmor is a song, framed with skill, and sung to God by His people.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the centrality of sung praise, and the abiding worth of the inspired Psalter. The people of God are a singing people; they are to praise Him with melody and skill, the truth borne upon a tune. The apostle keeps the mizmor in the church’s hand, bidding her sing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs; and the Book of Psalms remains her first and surest songbook, the mind of the Spirit set to music.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Hebrew for making music upon the strings, Mizmor is the word rendered “Psalm” — a song set to music for the worship of God.

Mizmor — Hebrew mizmōr, from zāmar, to make music or pluck the strings.

It is the very word the English “Psalm” translates.

It stands in the title of some fifty-seven psalms.

The Greek rendered it psalmos, whence comes our word Psalter.

The apostle keeps it in the church: psalms and hymns and spiritual songs (Eph 5:19).
